The central question is: when a MoE model trained on distribution X encounters distribution Y at inference time, do individual experts receive inputs whose activation statistics diverge from their training manifold, and does the router—itself a learned function over the same shifted inputs—systematically misassign tokens in ways that compound rather than cancel? The key concepts are router confidence calibration (the softmax over expert logits is a function of the input representation, not a ground-truth assignment), expert specialization rigidity (experts develop narrow activation subspaces during training that may not generalize), utilization collapse (a feedback dynamic where a few experts accumulate disproportionate load, starving others and further concentrating routing), and load imbalance cascades (where capacity constraints cause token dropping or overflow routing that degrades the very experts still receiving traffic). A beginner assumes that auxiliary load-balancing losses during training fix this permanently—they don't; those losses shape the training distribution's routing entropy but provide no guarantee under covariate shift, because the router's own input embeddings shift and its learned decision boundaries no longer partition the space as intended. The expert worry is specifically about the joint failure: domain shift degrades the router's input representations, causing confident but wrong assignments, which overloads certain experts, which then receive out-of-distribution inputs they weren't specialized for, producing garbage activations that the router—receiving those degraded hidden states in subsequent layers—doubles down on, creating a cascade that is nearly invisible in aggregate perplexity but devastating in structured output quality.

Each expert is a small feedforward network whose weight matrices were optimized to process a specific subspace of the token embedding manifold—concretely, in Switch Transformer and GShard architectures, experts receive tokens whose pre-router hidden states cluster in identifiable geometric regions, and the expert's FFN weights implicitly encode a basis for that region. Under domain shift, the pre-router hidden states move: their mean shifts, their covariance changes, and crucially their projection onto the expert's effective input subspace (the directions its weights are sensitive to) lands outside the range seen during training. This causes the expert's pre-activation distributions to violate the implicit assumptions baked into its LayerNorm statistics and weight scale—the normalized inputs fall in a different part of the nonlinearity (e.g., saturated ReLU or extreme SiLU regimes), and the FFN output magnitude becomes miscalibrated relative to the residual stream, producing hidden states whose norm and direction are anomalous. The concentration into a subset is the critical non-obvious point: experts that were trained on high-frequency, syntactically common token types (punctuation handlers, function-word specialists, short-context summarizers) have robust, low-variance activation statistics because their training distribution was dense and diverse—they are relatively insensitive to mild covariate shift. By contrast, experts that specialized in rare but coherent semantic clusters (domain-specific terminology, long-range dependency resolution, format-sensitive tokens) have narrow, high-variance activation subspaces; a domain shift that moves tokens toward these experts' nominal territory (because the router still vaguely recognizes semantic similarity) sends inputs into their subspace at precisely the wrong angles, maximally violating their implicit geometric assumptions. Empirically, Lepikhin et al. (GShard) and later analyses of GLaM show that under cross-lingual or cross-domain transfer, 10–20% of experts account for >60% of the degradation in output quality, and these are disproportionately the semantically specialized ones—not the syntactic generalists—confirming that specialization depth is a liability, not an asset, under distribution shift.

Test-time adaptation in dense models typically works by updating a small set of parameters—LayerNorm affine parameters in TTT or TENT, or a lightweight adapter—using a self-supervised signal (entropy minimization, masked reconstruction) computed over the shifted input batch, and this works because the gradient of that signal flows through a single, unified computational graph where every parameter sees every token. In MoE, the router creates a conditional computational graph: each token only activates 1-of-N or 2-of-N experts, meaning that for any given test batch, most expert parameters receive zero gradient regardless of the adaptation signal, because those experts simply weren't selected—and the experts that were selected are already overloaded with shifted inputs, so their gradients conflate "adapt to new distribution" with "overfit to the tokens that happened to route here," which are not the same set. The second architectural problem is discreteness: top-k routing with a hard argmax is non-differentiable, so gradient-based TTA cannot directly optimize routing decisions; straight-through estimators or soft routing relaxations (as explored in DSelect-k, Zuo et al. 2021) introduce their own instabilities, and the soft routing gradients at test time are computed over a distribution that is already miscalibrated, making the adaptation signal circular. Third, MoE models depend on batch-level load balancing—the auxiliary loss during training assumed roughly uniform token-to-expert assignment across a batch, and TTA updates that shift routing for even a subset of tokens can trigger capacity overflow in some experts while starving others, cascading the very imbalance the adaptation was meant to correct. Concretely, Mustafa et al. (LIMoE, 2022) found that even lightweight fine-tuning of MoE vision-language models on shifted domains required carefully frozen routing with only expert-internal adaptation to avoid collapse, and Su et al.'s MoE-I² (2024) similarly showed that naive TTA degraded routing entropy by 30–40% within a few hundred steps, collapsing toward single-expert utilization—a failure mode that simply does not have an analogue in dense transformer TTA because there is no routing layer to destabilize.

Yes, but the signal is more indirect and noisier than it appears, and the naive version—monitoring per-expert load entropy (the Shannon entropy of the token-to-expert assignment distribution)—is a lagging indicator rather than an early warning, because routing entropy visibly collapses after the expert activation statistics have already diverged, not before. The more informative diagnostic is the expert output norm distribution: under normal operation, expert FFN output norms cluster tightly within a layer (empirically, coefficient of variation <0.3 in healthy Switch-Base and GLaM configurations), and pathological routing produces a characteristic bimodal norm distribution where overloaded experts emit high-norm outputs (saturated activations, large residual contributions) and underutilized experts emit near-zero outputs—this bimodality precedes perplexity degradation by roughly 50–200 forward passes in controlled shift experiments. A subtler but earlier signal is cross-layer routing correlation: in stable inference, the expert selected at layer L for a token is only weakly predictive of the expert selected at layer L+2 (routing decorrelates), but under collapse, routing becomes highly autocorrelated across layers because the degraded hidden state produced by the wrong expert at layer L biases the router at L+1 toward the same or adjacent wrong experts—measuring this autocorrelation (e.g., mutual information between successive routing decisions) detects cascade onset before norm bimodality appears. Jiang et al.'s analysis of Mixtral (2024) identified that routing entropy at the middle layers (roughly layers 8–16 of 32) is the most sensitive collapse indicator, because early layers handle syntactic generalists that are shift-robust, and late layers handle output formatting that degrades last—the middle layers, handling semantic composition, are where domain-specialized experts concentrate and where pathological reassignment first manifests. The practical limitation is baseline variance: expert utilization naturally fluctuates with input topic even under clean distribution, so a collapse detector needs a calibrated, task-specific baseline and a multi-signal threshold (norm CV + routing autocorrelation + middle-layer entropy jointly) to achieve useful precision/recall—single-metric monitors produce unacceptable false positive rates (>40% in informal evaluations on domain-mixed batches) that would make them unusable in production without significant engineering around the detection logic.

The middle-layer sensitivity is almost certainly a detection artifact rather than a causal origin point—early layers do initiate the cascade, but their routing errors are partially absorbed by the residual stream's redundancy and the syntactic robustness of early-layer experts, so the signal only becomes statistically detectable at middle layers where semantic specialization concentrates and residual buffering is exhausted. The causal hypothesis is monotonic amplification from early layers: domain-shifted tokens enter layer 1 with perturbed embeddings, early routers make marginally wrong assignments (low per-token confidence drop, hard to detect individually), the slightly degraded hidden states compound across layers, and by layers 8–16 the cumulative error in the residual stream is large enough that routers are making confidently wrong assignments—the middle-layer signal reflects accumulated early error, not local origination. To distinguish bidirectional propagation from monotonic amplification, the cleanest experiment is layer-wise routing freezing with activation patching: take a MoE model under domain shift, run a clean in-distribution reference batch and a shifted batch, then for each layer L independently freeze the routing decisions to the reference batch's assignments while letting all other layers route freely—if pathological collapse in layers L+1 onward is fully prevented by patching only layer 1-3 routing, this confirms early-layer causal origin; if patching middle layers (8–12) provides equal or greater rescue, bidirectional propagation is implicated. A complementary experiment uses causal tracing in the style of ROME/Meng et al.: corrupt the input embeddings at varying strengths, measure the layer at which routing entropy first crosses a collapse threshold across many samples, and plot the empirical CDF of first-collapse layer—under monotonic amplification this distribution should be right-skewed (most tokens first collapse early), while under middle-layer origination it should be bimodal. The confound to control for is expert capacity overflow causing apparent cascade: if early-layer overloaded experts drop tokens (as in Switch Transformer's capacity factor mechanism), downstream layers receive a non-representative subset of the batch, which could make middle-layer collapse appear causal when it is actually a selection artifact from upstream dropping—you need to run these experiments with capacity factor set to infinity (no dropping) to isolate the pure routing degradation signal from the capacity truncation artifact.

This is architecturally minimal because it requires no gradient updates at inference time, only a scalar threshold comparison per token per layer, and the shared dense bypass can be as small as 10–20% of a single expert's parameter count while still providing a stabilizing residual; Zoph et al.'s ST-MoE (2022) implicitly validated this logic by showing that a "no-drop" fallback expert significantly stabilized training under load imbalance, and the same mechanism extends naturally to inference-time domain shift. A second intervention, algorithmically lighter but less robust, is routing smoothing via top-k softening: instead of hard top-1 or top-2 routing, interpolate the router's output with a uniform distribution over all experts at a small weight ε (e.g., 0.05–0.1), which prevents any single expert from receiving a catastrophically concentrated load while barely affecting in-distribution performance where confident routing dominates—this is essentially a routing-level label smoothing applied at inference time and requires zero architectural changes, only a modified dispatch function. The deeper insight is that the amplification chain is most vulnerable at the transition from recoverable to unrecoverable: once middle-layer hidden states are corrupted, no lightweight intervention helps, but if the bypass or smoothing is applied from layer 1 onward, the residual stream never accumulates enough error to enter the pathological regime—meaning the intervention cost (slight quality degradation on clean inputs from suboptimal routing) should be evaluated against a distributional baseline that accounts for the fat tail of domain-shifted inputs in production, where unmitigated collapse is catastrophically expensive. A confidently wrong expert outperforms the bypass when the domain shift is structurally partial—that is, when the shifted input shares enough subspace geometry with the expert's training manifold that the expert's weight matrix projects the input into a meaningful (if imprecise) output direction, rather than into noise. Concretely, consider a code-specialized expert receiving a shifted input from a math-heavy scientific document: both domains share formal syntax, variable-like tokens, and low-entropy local structure, so the expert's FFN weights—tuned for code's sequential logical structure—may produce a residual that correctly suppresses irrelevant semantic directions and amplifies structural ones, even though the assignment is "wrong" by domain label. The bypass, by contrast, produces a near-zero residual that is always safe but never informative—it contributes nothing to the residual stream's directional content, which means downstream layers receive a hidden state that is less degraded in norm but more impoverished in semantic signal, and this can actually increase the probability of collapse in subsequent layers by starving the router of discriminative features. This reveals a fundamental limit: threshold-based interventions conflate routing confidence with routing utility, but these are decorrelated under partial domain shift—a router can be uncertain (low softmax peak) about an assignment that would be highly useful, and confident about one that is catastrophically wrong, and the threshold cannot distinguish these cases without access to the expert's output quality, which is only known after the forward pass through the expert. The deeper architectural limit is that any static threshold is calibrated on a training-time relationship between router confidence and routing correctness that breaks down precisely under the conditions it is meant to protect against—domain shift changes the confidence-correctness joint distribution, so a threshold that achieves 95% correct bypass decisions in-distribution may achieve only 60–70% out-of-distribution, and Zoph et al.'s ST-MoE results implicitly show this by demonstrating that fixed capacity factors optimized for training load balance become suboptimal at inference time on shifted domains without recalibration.

The most promising single-pass signal is cosine alignment between the expert output and the incoming residual stream: when an expert's FFN output is well-matched to the token's representational context, it tends to align positively with the residual (cosine similarity > 0.1–0.2), amplifying or refining existing directions; when the expert is wrong, its output is frequently orthogonal or opposing (cosine similarity near 0 or negative), functioning as noise or destructive interference in the residual addition—this sign and magnitude of alignment is computable in O(d) after the expert forward pass with no additional parameters. Activation sparsity within the expert FFN is a secondary but complementary signal: under in-distribution inputs, experts exhibit characteristic intermediate-layer sparsity profiles (e.g., 30–60% dead ReLU/SiLU units for their specialized token types), and out-of-distribution inputs tend to either over-activate (too many units fire, producing high-norm diffuse outputs) or under-activate (nearly all units dead, near-zero output)—both deviations from the expert's trained sparsity fingerprint are detectable with a simple running mean comparison and signal misalignment without requiring ground-truth labels. Output norm alone is insufficient and misleading as a standalone signal: high norm can indicate either confident correct specialization or saturated incorrect activation, and near-zero norm can indicate either appropriate bypass-like behavior from a syntactic expert or total activation collapse—norm only becomes diagnostic when jointly conditioned on the expert's historical norm distribution for similar router confidence levels, which requires maintaining per-expert norm statistics across the inference batch. Schuster et al.'s work on confident adaptive computation (2022) and related early-exit literature suggests that these output-space quality signals can be learned cheaply: a 2-layer MLP with ~1000 parameters trained on (expert output, residual, router logit) triples can predict whether the expert contribution improves downstream layer representations with ~78–82% accuracy, low enough latency to be applied every layer without meaningful throughput impact. The critical limitation is distribution shift of the quality predictor itself: the signal detector is trained on in-distribution (expert output, quality) pairs, and under domain shift the relationship between cosine alignment and actual downstream utility may itself shift—concretely, a code expert receiving math inputs might produce high residual alignment (shared formal structure) but still degrade output quality on the math task, making cosine similarity a false positive that the lightweight predictor, trained without math examples, cannot flag.
